document.summary: Fifteen Ethiopian sorghum cultivars plus one maize and one tef variety were processed into traditional foods (fermented flatbread, unleavened flatbread, porridge, dry-cooked grain) prepared as by local communities, and raw flour and foods were analysed for pepsin in vitro protein digestibility (IVPD), kafirin content (RP-HPLC), phytic acid, phytase, trypsin inhibitor activity, Fe and Zn. Cooking reduced IVPD in all genotypes, most in unfermented wet-cooked products, with a highly significant genotype x food product interaction so that genotype rankings changed between foods. Raw flour IVPD correlated negatively with protein, total kafirin and gamma-kafirin content, and processing, especially fermentation, lowered phytic acid and phytate/mineral ratios while raising Fe content.
key_findings: Raw flour IVPD ranged from 27.7% in the high tannin cultivar Seredo to 75.1% in the high lysine cultivar Wetet Be-gunchie, versus 55.8% in maize and 62.3% in tef.
Mean sorghum IVPD fell from 48.7% in raw flour to 27.8% in dry-cooked grain, 19.1% in fermented flatbread and about 13% in porridge and unleavened flatbread.
Genotype, food product and their interaction had highly significant effects on IVPD, and no cultivar had consistently high IVPD across all food products.
Only the high tannin cultivar Seredo was consistently among the lowest IVPD in raw flour and all cooked products.
Raw flour IVPD correlated negatively with total protein (r2 = 0.38), total kafirin (r2 = 0.66) and gamma-kafirin (r2 = 0.52); the kafirin association disappeared in fermented bread.
Wetet Be-gunchie had the lowest total kafirin and gamma-kafirin (4.1%) despite intermediate protein content (13.1%), indicating more non-kafirin protein.
Trypsin inhibitor activity rose from 6.27 mg/g in raw flour to 6.81-7.16 mg/g in foods and correlated negatively with IVPD (r2 = 0.11).
Fermentation gave the lowest phytic acid (0.62 vs 0.77 g/100 g in raw flour), the highest phytase activity and the lowest phytate/Fe and phytate/Zn molar ratios.
Processing increased Fe by 20-44% and Zn by 4-29%, with fermentation having the greatest effect on Fe.
Amount of protein digested per 100 g flour differed little among most cultivars because high-protein cultivars had lower IVPD (e.g. Melkam 5.7 g vs Masugi-Yellow 6.1 g).

claims.subject: wet cooking
claims.statement: Wet cooking decreases sorghum protein digestibility.
claims.evidence: The best-known example of this for sorghum is the decrease in protein digestibility when sorghum is wet-cooked

claims.subject: phytic acid
claims.statement: Phytate-protein complexes make proteins less digestible, and phytate also chelates iron and zinc.
claims.evidence: While phytate-protein complexes make proteins less digestible, phytate also chelates iron and zinc hindering both macro and micronutrient bioavailability

claims.subject: protein digestibility
claims.statement: IVPD was determined by the pepsin digestibility method.
claims.context: raw flour and food samples; nitrogen by LECO combustion
claims.evidence: In-vitro protein digestibility (IVPD) was determined according to the pepsin digestibility method

claims.subject: tannin
claims.statement: Tannin concentration was measured by the HCl vanillin assay.
claims.evidence: Tannin concentration of the raw flour and food samples was determined using HCl vannillin assay

claims.subject: phytic acid content
claims.statement: Phytic acid was measured with a commercial Megazyme colorimetric kit.
claims.evidence: Measurement of phytic acid was done using a commercial colorimetric kit

claims.subject: iron content
claims.statement: Fe and Zn were analysed by inductively coupled plasma spectrometry after nitric-perchloric acid digestion.
claims.evidence: Analysis for Fe and Zn was carried out using an Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) Spectrometer

claims.subject: kafirin content
claims.statement: Kafirin content and composition of raw flours were analysed by RP-HPLC on a C18 column.
claims.evidence: Raw flour samples were analyzed for kafirin content and composition using RP-HPLC with a C18 column

claims.subject: Masugi-Yellow
claims.statement: Masugi-Yellow had the lowest protein content among the 15 cultivars.
claims.evidence: The protein content among cultivars ranged from a low of 9.8% in one of the farmers’ variety Masugi-Yellow, to a high of 15.2% in the high tannin red variety, Seredo.

claims.subject: Seredo
claims.statement: The high tannin red variety Seredo had the highest protein content among the 15 cultivars.
claims.evidence: The protein content among cultivars ranged from a low of 9.8% in one of the farmers’ variety Masugi-Yellow, to a high of 15.2% in the high tannin red variety, Seredo.

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: The high lysine cultivar Wetet Be-gunchie had an intermediate protein content.
claims.evidence: The high lysine cultivar, Wetet Be-gunchie, has an intermediate protein content of 13.1%.

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: Wetet Be-gunchie had the lowest gamma-kafirin content among the cultivars.
claims.context: raw flour; RP-HPLC; vs 7.5% in Teshale
claims.evidence: Likewise, the γ-kafirin content among cultivars ranged from 4.1% in Wetet Be-gunchie to 7.5% in variety Teshale which also had the highest total kafirin.

claims.subject: Teshale
claims.statement: Teshale had the highest gamma-kafirin content and the highest total kafirin.
claims.evidence: Likewise, the γ-kafirin content among cultivars ranged from 4.1% in Wetet Be-gunchie to 7.5% in variety Teshale which also had the highest total kafirin.

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: Despite intermediate protein content, Wetet Be-gunchie had the lowest total kafirin, indicating a significant portion of non-kafirin protein.
claims.evidence: Wetet Be-gunchie despite its intermediate protein content had the lowest amount of both total kafirin and γ-kafirin indicating that it carries significant portion of non-kafirin protein.

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: Sorghum IVPD decreased in all food products, least in dry-cooked food, then fermented bread, and most in unfermented wet-cooked products.
claims.context: 15 sorghum cultivars; traditional Ethiopian foods; pepsin assay
claims.value: mean 48.7% raw; 27.8% dry-cooked; 19.1% fermented flatbread; 13.2% porridge; 13.3% unleavened flatbread
claims.evidence: Sorghum IVPD decreased in food products with dry cooked food having relatively higher IVPD followed by fermented bread, and the unfermented wet-cooked products having the least IVPD (Table 3).

claims.subject: Chiro
claims.statement: Chiro, Teshale and IS9302 had the higher IVPD of about 30% in dry-cooked samples, markedly below maize.
claims.evidence: In dry cooked samples, varieties Chiro, Teshale and the high tannin IS9302 had higher IVPD of about 30% which was markedly lower than ~40% in maize.

claims.subject: Meko
claims.statement: Meko had the highest sorghum IVPD in fermented bread, though well below maize and tef.
claims.evidence: While Meko had higher IVPD of 24% in fermented bread which is again considerably less than 45.4 and 33.8% in maize and tef, respectively.

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: In porridge and unleavened bread, high lysine Wetet Be-gunchie had higher IVPD than tef and other sorghum genotypes but lower than maize.
claims.evidence: The IVPD in the unfermented food products, porridge and unleavened bread, was higher in the high lysine Wetet Be-gunchie (26.6 and 19.1%, respectively) than tef and other sorghum genotypes but lower than that of maize.

claims.subject: IS9302
claims.statement: IVPD of IS9302 and Teshale was least affected by dry cooking, retaining most of the raw flour IVPD.
claims.context: dry-cooked grain, as percent of raw flour IVPD; Teshale 77.3%
claims.evidence: Accordingly, the IVPD in IS9302 and Teshale were least affected by dry cooking that they maintained 82 and 77.3%, respectively, of the IVPD of the raw flour.

claims.context: dry-cooked grain, as percent of raw flour IVPD; Wetet Be-gunchie 39%
claims.evidence: Whereas, the high lysine cultivar Wetet Be-gunchie and Degalit-Yellow maintained only 39 and 38.3%, respectively, of the digestibility of the raw

claims.subject: Zea mays
claims.statement: Maize IVPD was least affected by processing, with fermented bread not differing from raw flour.
claims.context: maize Melkassa-2 vs tef and sorghum; traditional foods
claims.evidence: Maize was least affected by processing methods with IVPD in raw maize sample not significantly different from the fermented bread but lower in other food products (Fig 1).

claims.subject: Seredo
claims.statement: Only the high tannin Seredo was consistently among the lowest IVPD in all cooked products and raw flour.
claims.context: all four food products and raw flour
claims.evidence: Only Seredo was consistently grouped among the low IVPD category in all cooked products as well as the raw flour.

claims.evidence: As expected, there were positive correlations between total protein and total kafirin (r2 = 0.72) as well as total protein and γ-kafirin (r2 = 0.44) (Fig 4).

claims.subject: protein content
claims.statement: Total protein correlated positively with gamma-kafirin.
claims.evidence: As expected, there were positive correlations between total protein and total kafirin (r2 = 0.72) as well as total protein and γ-kafirin (r2 = 0.44) (Fig 4).

claims.subject: protein content
claims.statement: Raw flour IVPD correlated significantly and negatively with total protein.
claims.evidence: Correlations of raw flour IVPD with total protein (r2 = 0.38), total kafirin (r2 = 0.66) and γ-kafirin (r2 = 0.52) were significant and negative

claims.subject: kafirin content
claims.statement: Raw flour IVPD correlated significantly and negatively with total kafirin.
claims.evidence: Correlations of raw flour IVPD with total protein (r2 = 0.38), total kafirin (r2 = 0.66) and γ-kafirin (r2 = 0.52) were significant and negative

claims.evidence: Correlations of raw flour IVPD with total protein (r2 = 0.38), total kafirin (r2 = 0.66) and γ-kafirin (r2 = 0.52) were significant and negative

claims.evidence: as was IVPD of unleavened flatbread and porridge with total kafirin (r2 = 0.18 and r2 = 0.14, respectively)

claims.subject: raw protein digestibility
claims.statement: Raw flour IVPD correlated positively with porridge and unleavened flatbread IVPD.
claims.context: 15 sorghum cultivars; porridge and unleavened flatbread
claims.evidence: Raw flour IVPD showed positive correlation with porridge IVPD (r2 = 0.48) and unleavened flatbread (r2 = 0.49).

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: Trypsin inhibitor activity was significantly lower in raw flour and increased during food processing.
claims.value: 6.27 mg/g raw flour vs 6.81-7.16 mg/g in foods
claims.evidence: Trypsin inhibitor activity was significantly lower in raw flour and increased during food processing.

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Fermentation considerably reduced phytic acid.
claims.context: fermented flatbread vs raw flour, across genotypes
claims.evidence: Fermentation appeared to have positive effect on enhancing protein nutrition in that it considerably reduced phytic acid and TIA, and significantly improved phytase activity (Table 5).

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Fermentation significantly improved phytase activity.
claims.context: fermented flatbread vs raw flour, across genotypes
claims.evidence: Fermentation appeared to have positive effect on enhancing protein nutrition in that it considerably reduced phytic acid and TIA, and significantly improved phytase activity (Table 5).

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Phytate/Fe and phytate/Zn molar ratios were highest in raw flour and lowest in fermented flatbread.
claims.context: across genotype means; order raw flour > porridge > unleavened flatbread > dry-cooked > fermented flatbread
claims.evidence: phytate/Fe and phytate/Zn molar ratios showed a consistent pattern with raw flour > porridge > unleavened flatbread > dry-cooked > fermented flatbread (Table 5)

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: Wetet Be-gunchie had consistently and significantly higher phytic acid than Degalit-Yellow and Chiro in raw flour and all cooked products.
claims.evidence: Phytic acid concentration was consistently and significantly higher in Wetet Be-gunchie in both raw flour and all of the cooked products

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: Wetet Be-gunchie had higher phytase activity than Degalit-Yellow and Chiro except in fermented flatbread and dry-cooked product.
claims.context: compared with Degalit-Yellow and Chiro; n.s. in fermented flatbread and dry-cooked grain
claims.evidence: Wetet Be-gunchie also showed higher levels of phytase activity in all products except in the fermented flat bread and dry-cooked product where the difference was not significant (Fig 5B).

claims.subject: Wetet Be-gunchie
claims.statement: Trypsin inhibitor activity did not differ among the three high-IVPD cultivars except in porridge, where Wetet Be-gunchie was significantly lower.
claims.context: porridge; compared with Degalit-Yellow and Chiro
claims.evidence: Trypsin inhibitor on the other hand was not significant between the three genotypes except in the cooked product porridge where Wetet Be-gunchie was shown to be significantly lower than the other genotypes

claims.subject: phytic acid content
claims.statement: Raw flour IVPD showed a significant positive correlation with phytic acid.
claims.evidence: While the raw flour IVPD showed significant and positive correlation with phytic acid (r2 = 0.03)

claims.subject: trypsin inhibitor activity
claims.statement: Trypsin inhibitory activity showed a significant negative correlation with IVPD.
claims.evidence: trypsin inhibitory activity showed a significant and negative correlation with IVPD (r2 = 0.11)

claims.subject: phytase activity
claims.statement: Phytase activity correlated positively with Fe content.
claims.evidence: Correlations of phytase with Fe (r2 = 0.10) and Zn content (r2 = 0.06), and Fe with Zn (r2 = 0.10) were positive.

claims.subject: phytase activity
claims.statement: Phytase activity correlated positively with Zn content.
claims.evidence: Correlations of phytase with Fe (r2 = 0.10) and Zn content (r2 = 0.06), and Fe with Zn (r2 = 0.10) were positive.

claims.subject: phytic acid content
claims.statement: Phytic acid correlated negatively with trypsin inhibitory activity.
claims.evidence: Moreover, phytic acid showed a negative correlation with trypsin inhibitory activity (r2 = 0.05).

claims.subject: dry cooking
claims.statement: Unlike earlier reports of no negative effect, dry cooking (popping or roasting) reduced IVPD in all sorghum varieties and in maize.
claims.context: dry-cooked intact grain; 15 sorghum cultivars and maize
claims.evidence: Earlier studies have reported popping or roasting to have no negative effect on sorghum IVPD [43] but in this study it did affect IVPD in all sorghum varieties as well as in maize genotype.

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Fermentation increases sorghum IVPD compared with unfermented wet-cooked products such as porridge and unleavened bread.
claims.context: compared with unfermented wet cooking; also seen here (19.1% fermented flatbread vs ~13% porridge and unleavened flatbread)
claims.evidence: Several other investigations have shown fermentation to increase the IVPD of sorghum [39,65–67] compared to unfermented wet-cooking such as in unleavened bread and porridge which severely reduces digestibility

claims.subject: tannin
claims.statement: High tannin genotypes had consistently lower IVPD in all food products as well as raw flour.
claims.context: high tannin genotypes (Seredo); raw flour and all cooked products
claims.evidence: The only exception was the high tannin genotypes that had consistently lower IVPD in all food products as well as the raw sample.

claims.subject: gamma-kafirin
claims.statement: Gamma-kafirin is resistant to pepsin due to its high cysteine content leading to disulfide cross-links, consistent with its negative association with IVPD.
claims.evidence: The negative association between γ-kafirin and IVPD agrees with the previous reports that γ-kafirin is resistant to pepsin owing to its high cysteine content that leads to disulphide cross-links

claims.subject: kafirin content
claims.statement: After cooking, the association between IVPD and protein or kafirin content was markedly weaker and absent in fermented breads.
claims.evidence: However, when the flour was cooked to different food products, the strength of the association between IVPD and protein/kafirin content also markedly reduced with the association becoming non-existent in fermented breads.

claims.subject: Melkam
claims.statement: Melkam flour, with 15% protein and 38% IVPD, yields 5.7 g protein digested per 100 g.
claims.context: raw flour; computed from protein content and IVPD
claims.evidence: For example, 100g of flour from variety Melekam (15% protein content) at the reported IVPD of 38% yields 5.7g protein digested.

claims.subject: Masugi-Yellow
claims.statement: Low protein Masugi-Yellow with 61% IVPD yields 6.1 g protein digested per 100 g flour, similar to the low digestible Melkam.
claims.context: raw flour; computed from protein content and IVPD; vs Melkam 5.7 g
claims.evidence: A low protein (10%) cultivar such as Masugi-Yellow with a reported IVPD of 61% has a yield of 6.1g protein digested, not very different from the low digestible Melekam with the higher total protein.

claims.subject: Ethiopian sorghum cultivars
claims.statement: The amount of protein digested per unit flour was not very different among genotypes except Wetet Be-gunchie and Seredo.
claims.context: raw flours; exceptions high lysine Wetet Be-gunchie and high tannin Seredo
claims.evidence: When the amount digested is considered, the amount of protein digested per unit of flour/food sample was not very different between genotypes except for the high lysine Wetet Be-gunchie and the high tannin Seredo in raw flours.

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: The IVPD reduction in fermented products may result from cooking altering protein structures through disulfide cross-linking or increased hydrophobicity.
claims.evidence: The absolute reduction in IVPD of fermented product, however, has to do with the cooking of the protein that may have resulted in altered protein structures through disulfide cross linking or increased hydrophobicity

claims.evidence: the positive effects of cooking on phytic acid were compromised by increased TIA in all products which along with other chemical changes to the protein body and starch-protein complex may have undermined the overall digestibility in cooked products

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Cooking markedly increased total Fe content, with fermentation having the greatest effect.
claims.context: fermented flatbread vs raw flour, across genotypes
claims.evidence: Cooking seem to have markedly increased total Fe content with fermentation having the greatest effect (Table 5).

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: Processing increased iron levels by 20-44%, perhaps due to phytic acid degradation.
claims.context: traditional food products vs raw flour
claims.evidence: Processing increased mineral levels by 20–44% for iron and 4–29% for zinc perhaps due to degradation of phytic acid.

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: Processing increased zinc levels by 4-29%, perhaps due to phytic acid degradation.
claims.context: traditional food products vs raw flour
claims.evidence: Processing increased mineral levels by 20–44% for iron and 4–29% for zinc perhaps due to degradation of phytic acid.

claims.subject: phytic acid
claims.statement: Phytate binds minerals and strongly compromises Fe and Zn bioavailability.
claims.evidence: Due to its high density of negatively charged phosphate groups, phytate binds with minerals and inhibit their availability, especially Fe and Zn bioavailability have been reported to be highly compromised by phytic acid

claims.subject: fermentation
claims.statement: Based on phytate/mineral ratios, predicted Fe and Zn availability followed fermented bread > dry cooked > wet-cooked > raw flour.
claims.context: estimated from phytate/mineral molar ratios, not measured directly
claims.evidence: Based on the phytate/mineral ratio in the current study, the trend in the availability of Fe and Zn follows the order of fermented bread > dry cooked > wet-cooked > raw flour.

claims.subject: cooking
claims.statement: Genotype, food processing method and their interaction had highly significant effects on IVPD of Ethiopian traditional sorghum foods.
claims.context: 15 cultivars x 4 foods + raw flour; genotype x food product interaction P < 0.001
claims.evidence: The study showed that both genotype, food processing method and their intercation have highly significant effect on IVPD of sorghum traditional foods commonly used by rural communities in Ethiopia.
